Balancing speed and accuracy

A suitable path depends on the function, the input range, and the error the application can tolerate. For vector calls, it also depends on which inputs share a block. The Technical Guide summarizes how to make that choice. The measurements and calculations below show how it changes with the workload.

Two gains account for the results. A faster scalar method benefits every call that can use it, including scalar evaluation inside a batch. A native batch can offer a further gain. On the matched dense inputs, the eleven Double64 elementary batches were 2.96–3.59× faster than current scalar evaluation and returned identical output words. Six Double32 native batches were 1.44–2.70× faster than current scalar evaluation and had higher sampled maximum errors. The larger before/after gains in the manual include changes to the scalar baseline. Technical Guide benchmarks

Reading the measurements

The matched run used revision 2d860805, Julia 1.10.10 with a native CPU target, and one thread on an Intel i9-14900K. Each case used 32,768 inputs and preallocated outputs. Times are medians of nine interleaved timing samples, with eight calls per sample. The scalar loop calls the public function on each input. The batch uses serial DoubleFloats.simdmap! on dense, disjoint vectors and includes eligibility checks and fallback. A ratio close to 1× means the measured times were close. For example, the Double32 exp2 dense scalar and batch medians differ by 0.066 ns per element, while the batch's interquartile range spans 0.139 ns per element. Treat small differences of this size as timing-sensitive.

For a finite, nonzero reference $y$, the score is $E=|\widehat y-y|/(|y|\epsilon_D)$. The working-precision unit $\epsilon_D$ is $2^{-104}$ for Double64 and $2^{-46}$ for Double32, so compare their scores to targets in their respective units. The reference uses both input words and 512-bit BigFloat arithmetic. The tables show the 99th percentile (p99) and the maximum of each sample. Tuple results use the largest component score per input. Complex results use the complex magnitude. A sampled maximum gives evidence for the tested inputs. A domain-wide bound requires further analysis. Accuracy Report

The largest gains come from doing less arithmetic in a range where a simpler evaluation is accurate enough. Double64 uses fine tables and short reductions for the exponentials and logarithms, dyadic anchors for atan, and bounded direct approximations for tan and the hyperbolic functions. The measured Double64 sinh maximum fell from 2.322 to 0.397 units, and tan fell from 1.229 to 0.358, while both got faster. For exp and exp2, the faster methods raised the sampled maxima from 0.831 to 0.938 and 0.837 to 1.009 respectively. The expm1 maximum fell slightly, from 1.603 to 1.579, while p99 rose from 0.901 to 1.073. A tail-percentile target and a maximum target therefore give different assessments of that change. Scalar implementation details

For Double32, widening is fast when the sum of the words is exactly representable in Float64 and the result is in a safe range for splitting back into two Float32 words. All eleven dense fixtures admitted 32,103 of 32,768 inputs to this scalar route. Some low words were too sparse to survive widening. The largest scalar Double32 exp2 error came from the fallback at the pair (1.7698154f0, 3.6909767f-10). The exp2 maximum nevertheless fell from 0.911 to 0.614 units on the matched inputs. Its p99 fell from 0.442 to 0.113.

The same input conversion error can matter much more near a root. If rounding the input changes $x$ by $\delta$, the first-order relative change in $f(x)$ is about $|f'(x)/f(x)|\,|\delta|$ when $f(x)\ne0$. For exp the factor $|f'(x)/f(x)|$ is one. For log and log2 it grows as $1/|x-1|$ near one. For example, Double32(1.0f0, Float32(2^-60)) has a logarithm of approximately $2^{-60}$, which would disappear if conversion rounded the input to one. The two-word path retains it. Exact widening removes this input error. The subsequent function evaluation and split still round. Double32 implementation details

Several functions preserve accuracy by keeping a small quantity explicit. expm1 carries the offset from one through reconstruction. log1p starts with $x$ rather than first forming $1+x$. sinh keeps $x$ as its leading term. The local tan and tanh formulas carry a small correction to $x$. The tan fallback pays for more accurate phase reduction near poles. For cosh, an even expansion or guarded widening makes ordinary scalar evaluation cheap. Elementary function algorithms

At exponential underflow, the least positive subnormal $\Delta$ sets the spacing that can be represented in the result. Half a grid step corresponds to $\Delta/(2|y|\epsilon_D)$ in relative working-precision units. This quantity grows as the reference shrinks. Use nearest-grid agreement, absolute error, and zero or overflow classification at the format limits. The targeted exp and exp2 probes in the Accuracy Report agreed with the nearest grid on all 22 subnormal or grid-limited inputs per operation and format. Exponential rounding analysis

The gains depend on what the batch can simplify. For example, a constant exponent of 5 selects a short chain of squarings and multiplications. A vector of exponents uses the positive-base logarithm/exponential composition. Bounded inputs keep intermediate values in range for hypot and paired normalize. The incremental gains for sincos and cis were modest on this compiler target. Binary atan, sqrt, square, and abs2 ran near scalar throughput in these fixtures. Comparing accuracy and speed together

Start with requirements that every candidate must satisfy. These may include signed zero, domain behavior, assignment order, overlap, and a hard accuracy ceiling. The measurements give a sample-based screen for the numerical requirements. At a 1.52-unit maximum, all six native Double32 kernels pass the dense sampled screen. Double64 expm1, coth, asech, and integer power with exponent 5 exceed that ceiling on their tested inputs. These cases pass the 2.2-unit screen. At 1.0 unit, the Double32 log1p batch and Double64 exp2, expm1, and log1p exceed the dense sampled ceiling. The Double64 scalar and batch words agree for those operations, so switching the execution route gives the same sampled error.

Use the hard ceiling to rule out any route that misses it. If a remaining route is faster with equal or smaller error, it can be chosen directly for the measured workload. A weighted crossover helps when one route is faster and the other is more accurate. Test sensitive regions and input layouts separately before applying that choice to a broader workload.

After screening, a graded comparison can express how well each candidate fits the workload. The categories include function, format, range, input arrangement, storage, and target.

Normalizing time and error

\[\begin{aligned} q_k &= \frac{\sigma T_k}{T_s}, \\ a_k &= \max \left\{\frac{E_{99,k}}{\tau_{99}}, \frac{E_{\max,k}}{\tau_{\max}}\right\}. \end{aligned}\]

Here $T_s$ is the scalar baseline time, $T_k$ is the candidate time, and $\sigma$ is the requested speedup. The two errors $E_{99,k}$ and $E_{\max,k}$ are the candidate's p99 and maximum. The corresponding targets are $\tau_{99}$ and $\tau_{\max}$.

The speed and accuracy grades $1/(1+q_k)$ and $1/(1+a_k)$ reach one half when the candidate meets the corresponding target exactly. For workload $c$, use the smallest grade across requirements.

\[Q(c,k) = \min \left\{I(c,k), \frac{1}{1+q_k}, \frac{1}{1+a_k}, \mu_C(c,k)\right\}.\]

The indicator $I$ is one for a candidate that passes the hard screen and zero otherwise. Set the coverage grade $\mu_C$ to one for ordinary timing comparisons, since coverage already affects the measured time. An explicit coverage requirement can grade candidates separately. Taking $\max_k Q(c,k)$ gives the best joint grade for that workload. These grades express chosen preferences and have no probability interpretation. Zadeh, Fuzzy Sets

For a concrete target, take $\sigma=2$, $\tau_{99}=1$, and $\tau_{\max}=2.2$. Dense Double32 log1p, sinh, and tanh meet all three targets. They miss the speed target with the mixed inputs. All eleven dense Double64 batches meet the speed and maximum targets. Only expm1 misses the p99 target, with an observed value of about 1.0735.

The accuracy weight at a crossover

A faster candidate with the same sampled error already wins on the time axis. When the faster route spends some accuracy margin, an explicit preference can resolve the choice. Give accuracy a weight $w$ between zero and one and minimize $L_w(k)=(1-w)\log q_k+w\log a_k$. Use a common positive floor for zero scores. A graded preference for $v$ over $s$ is $[1+\exp(L_w(v)-L_w(s))]^{-1}$. With $T_v<T_s$ and $a_v>a_s$, its midpoint is

\[w^*=\frac{\log(T_s/T_v)} {\log(T_s/T_v)+\log(a_v/a_s)}.\]

The crossover equates the gain in log time, $(1-w)\log(T_s/T_v)$, with the cost in log error, $w\log(a_v/a_s)$. The faster route wins below $w^*$ and the route with the lower normalized error score wins above it. Treat weights close to the crossover as sensitive to variation in timings or in the sampled errors. The table applies the formula to the same targets and shows how the choice moves when some lanes use scalar evaluation. The last column uses the maximum alone for the accuracy score.

How block coverage moves the crossover

If lanes are independent and each is eligible with probability $p$, a whole block of width $m$ is eligible with probability $b=p^m$. If each block needs one common regime, with disjoint regime probabilities $p_j$, then $b=\sum_j p_j^m$. Under that model, a 50/50 mix of two Double64 logarithm regimes gives $2^{1-32}$ for a 32-element block. Grouping those inputs into homogeneous blocks can restore the native path almost everywhere.

At a 1% miss rate, the model predicts 72.5% eligibility for 32-element blocks. The matched mixture admitted 740 of 1,024 such blocks, or 72.3%. With the same 328 replacements packed at the end of that array, only 11 blocks would contain misses, leaving 1,013 of 1,024 blocks eligible. The arrangement can therefore change native coverage from 72.3% to 98.9% at the same miss count. This is a block count, so the clustered speedup still needs to be measured. Sparse repair changes the condition to $K\le\lfloor m/8\rfloor$, where $K$ is the number of rejected lanes. Every rejected lane must also pass the repair safety check. Double64 exp2 and tan admitted all 512 blocks of width 64 in their mixed fixtures, with 245 using repair. Their speedups were 2.86× and 2.43×. In a separate Double32 experiment, scattering sparse low words while keeping the heads in range left the native kernels eligible. The source of a guard failure therefore matters alongside its frequency. Batch benchmark fixtures

For a rough prediction, let $N$ and $S$ be the fully eligible batch and fallback times per element. Let $H$ cover extra mixed execution overhead. If $N<S$, the condition for a speedup of at least $\sigma$ is approximately

\[\begin{aligned} T_v &\approx bN+(1-b)S+H, \\ b &\ge \frac{S(1-1/\sigma)+H}{S-N}. \end{aligned}\]

With $S=8.574$ ns and $N=3.170$ ns for Double32 tanh, setting $H=0$ requires about 79.3% eligible blocks for 2×. Under independence at width 32, that allows about 0.72% missed lanes. The actual mixed run reached 1.70×. Expensive outliers and repair can change the per-block cost, so measure them separately when they are common.

The error distribution also changes with coverage. If $\pi$ is the fraction of actual lanes that took native arithmetic and $F_n$ and $F_s$ are the conditional error distributions for native and scalar evaluation, then the fraction meeting an error threshold $e$ is

\[F_E(e) = \pi F_n(e) + (1-\pi)F_s(e).\]

The formula combines the two fractions at the same threshold. In the mixed Double32 log1p fixture, p99 improved from 0.578 to 0.544 and the maximum stayed at 1.151, while the speedup fell from 2.59× to 1.61×. The accuracy and speed measurements can therefore pull in opposite directions as coverage changes.

Finally, the batch driver checks axes and overlap before selecting a route. Views, overlapping inputs, and dense ranges shorter than 64 use scalar evaluation. Threading introduces separate size and exception-order constraints. These choices can move a workload past a crossover even when the numerical input range stays fixed. Vector API

Reproducing the comparison

Reset MersenneTwister(0xf01c) for each row and draw two vectors of 32,768 Float64 uniforms with rand(rng, n). For head interval (a, b) and underlying type F, pair the uniforms (u, v) to form h = F(a + (b - a)*u) and D(h, F(v - 0.5)*eps(h)). Draw independent input vectors in argument order, with the real part preceding the imaginary part in complex fixtures. For a mixed run, use positions randperm(rng, n)[1:328] after sampling the dense fixture and replace them with the heads above. Warm both entry points and alternate execution order when timing. Use the same inputs with the earlier revision for a before/after comparison.

This example recreates the dense and mixed Double32 tanh fixtures, times the two public evaluation routes, and computes the crossover. It reports a crossover only when the measured batch is faster and the scalar method has the lower error score. On the original run the dense maxima were 0.139 and 0.518 report units. Timings and the resulting crossover can vary with the machine and compiler.

using DoubleFloats, Random, Statistics

@noinline function scalar!(f::F, dest, x) where {F}
    @inbounds for i in eachindex(x)
        dest[i] = f(x[i])
    end
    return dest
end

@noinline function ns_per_element(apply::A, f::F, dest, x) where {A,F}
    start = time_ns()
    for _ in 1:8
        apply(f, dest, x)
    end
    return (time_ns() - start) / (8 * length(x))
end

function compare(f, x)
    scalar = scalar!(f, similar(x), x)
    batch = DoubleFloats.simdmap!(f, similar(x), x)
    scalar_times, batch_times = Float64[], Float64[]
    for i in 1:9
        if isodd(i)
            push!(scalar_times, ns_per_element(scalar!, f, scalar, x))
            push!(batch_times, ns_per_element(DoubleFloats.simdmap!, f, batch, x))
        else
            push!(batch_times, ns_per_element(DoubleFloats.simdmap!, f, batch, x))
            push!(scalar_times, ns_per_element(scalar!, f, scalar, x))
        end
    end
    times = (scalar=median(scalar_times), batch=median(batch_times))
    errors = setprecision(BigFloat, 512) do
        ref = f.(BigFloat.(x))
        map((scalar, batch)) do outputs
            e = [Float64(abs(BigFloat(y)-r) / (abs(r)*eps(Double32)))
                 for (y, r) in zip(outputs, ref)]
            (p99=quantile(e, 0.99), worst=maximum(e))
        end
    end
    a_s, a_v = map(e -> max(e.p99, e.worst / 2.2), errors)
    s, r = times.scalar / times.batch, a_v / a_s
    crossover = s > 1 && r > 1 ? log(s) / (log(s) + log(r)) : nothing
    return (; times, errors, speedup=s, crossover)
end

n = 32_768
rng = MersenneTwister(0xf01c)
a, b, replacement = 0.025, 0.95, 1.05
x = map(rand(rng, n), rand(rng, n)) do u, v
    h = Float32(a + (b - a) * u)
    Double32(h, Float32(v - 0.5) * eps(h))
end
println("dense  ", compare(tanh, x))
x[randperm(rng, n)[1:328]] .= Double32(replacement)
println("mixed  ", compare(tanh, x))

The benchmark driver supports varying input mixtures, storage, sizes, and threading. Keep input cohorts comparable. The local Double32 tan call took about 6 ns here. The broad benchmark report measured about 116 ns on a different distribution that exercises phase reduction and fallback. Benchmark Report
